source.title: Object Hallucination-Free Reinforcement Unlearning for Vision-Language Models
source.authors: Kaidi Jia; Yu-Jie Lin; Cheng-Yi Yang; Jia-Yao Ma; Jinsong Su

record.tranche_reason: Tests how unlearning and prompt-format changes affect concept recognition in vision-language models, a multimodal setting. It also compares encoder-based HFRU with transferred unlearning baselines.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own results for original, paraphrased, and discriminative prompts, and a qualitative hidden-state reconstruction. These bear on prompt-based recovery and representation-level forgetting. It does not test recovery by small fine-tuning sets, activation-direction ablation, or quantization. The hallucination scores and reward-component ablations do not by themselves test the claim versions about recovery.
record.test_reason: The study applies LLM unlearning baselines (GA, RMU and others) and its own encoder-only method (HFRU) to two vision-language models (Qwen2.5-VL-3B, Qwen3-VL-4B). It measures target-concept forgetting under original, paraphrased and discriminative prompts. That is a new multimodal setting with results on prompt-only recovery (E), on whether unlearning holds against simple attacks (A), and on a counter-method's robustness to those prompts (F). A qualitative hidden-state reconstruction bears weakly on C (access blocked versus features removed). There are no fine-tuning or quantization attacks.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors argue that decoder-centric unlearning gives superficial forgetting: visual representations persist and concepts resurface under discriminative prompts. They also argue it causes ungrounded hallucination. Their encoder-only GRPO method HFRU reaches over 98% forgetting and retention across prompt formats, with negligible hallucination and utility comparable to the base model. The record's paraphrase omits the hallucination emphasis, which is central to the paper.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes a two-stage vision-encoder method: cold-start alignment disruption followed by encoder-only GRPO with penalty, abstraction, and retention rewards. It also evaluates GA, RMU, and other transferred baselines in VLMs.
record.method_sensitivity: Prompt format changes outcomes substantially for some baselines. The paper also reports results across PACS, VGGFace2, and PACS-Sketch, and across Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct.

fits_no_version.finding: Unlearning induces object or identity hallucination. SimNPO reaches 100% hallucination on VGGFace2, and HFRU without the abstraction reward rises to 99.67% (Tables 2, 11).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Suppressing a concept without a semantic fallback makes models substitute ungrounded entities.

record.problems: The paper reports no error bars or statistical significance tests and states that it did not conduct such experiments because RL training was costly. The representation visualization is qualitative, and the reported evaluation covers two VLMs and specific datasets and prompt templates.
record.rows_left_out: The main tables report many additional baseline-method results and retention scores for each prompt condition. Not all were extracted: the selected rows prioritize explicit prompt-related recovery contrasts, HFRU results, and the qualitative representation comparison. No rows were included for unrelated hallucination-rate or reward-ablation metrics.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning, quantization or activation-ablation attacks. No chance-level or retrained-oracle reference; the forgetting metric is keyword absence in outputs.
Entirely untested: no relearning or fine-tuning attack after unlearning.
No activation-direction ablation or other internal edit to recover knowledge. Only a qualitative representation reconstruction.
Only one paraphrase template and one discriminative (yes/no) template per dataset. No jailbreaks, other languages or in-context information.
HFRU is tested only against prompt reformulation. Its resistance to relearning, internal edits and quantization is untested.

missing.what: Full-parameter (decoder-updated) HFRU variants show a sharp drop in forgetting under discriminative prompts versus encoder-only HFRU. This is direct evidence that decoder updates give prompt-recoverable forgetting.
Qwen3-VL-4B baseline results under prompt changes, e.g. GA PACS For. 100 (orig) → 10.00 (para) → 1.00 (disc); RMU PACS only 1.75 even at the original prompt.
Other Qwen2.5-VL baselines' prompt sensitivity, e.g. GD PACS 99.75→16.50 (para); SAUCE PACS 99.75→63.50 (para); SAUCE/GA PACS-Sketch discriminative drops to 41.89/12.43.

record.verdict_notes: Forgetting is measured as absence of the target keyword or its synonyms in a single sampled output. Collapsed models (GA/GD/RMU with near-zero retention) score high on forgetting trivially. Discriminative-prompt recovery for baselines may partly reflect yes-bias, since no absent-concept control is reported. There are no error bars. HFRU on Qwen3-VL VGGFace2 used full-parameter SFT, contrary to the encoder-only framing. The prompt 'attacks' are single templates, a weak test of E and F.

versions.untested_parts: The paper measures concept-forgetting, retention, and general utility across prompt formats, but does not establish a chance-level reference or compare against an oracle retrained model.
No post-unlearning recovery attack using a small unrelated, loosely related, or subset-of-forgotten-facts fine-tuning set.

No activation-direction ablation or recovery after an internal edit. The paper qualitatively compares reconstructed visual representations, rather than directly testing recovery of target behavior after an edit.
No low-bit quantization of unlearned weights.
Tests paraphrased and discriminative prompt formats. Does not test jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
Tests HFRU against paraphrased and discriminative prompting only; it does not test resistance to fine-tuning, activation ablation, or quantization attacks.

rows.measure: Qualitative change in reconstructed visual features for forget-set concepts
